utterances.speaker: JUDGE PARKER
utterances.text: Good afternoon. Unfortunately, Judge Van den Wyngaert is not feeling well and is unable to sit today. We hope that she'll be recovered enough to sit tomorrow. Judge Thelin and I will continue to sit under Rule 15 bis. Good afternoon, sir. May I remind you the affirmation you made at the beginning of your evidence still applies.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE PARKER
utterances.text: Ms. Residovic.

utterances.speaker: MS. RESIDOVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Thank you very much, Your Honours.

utterances.speaker: MS. RESIDOVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Good afternoon, Mr. Stojkov. Yesterday we were reviewing documents and you clarified them. The documents that you believe you saw during your stay at the OVR Cair and that you remember their contents and that you copied some of them. Do you remember that we discussed this towards the end of yesterday's evidence?

utterances.speaker: IGNO STOJKOV [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, I remember.

utterances.speaker: MS. RESIDOVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I would like to ask the usher to hand the set of documents to the witness again so that we can continue the questioning.

utterances.speaker: MS. RESIDOVIC
utterances.text: I will ask you, Mr. Stojkov, to find the document in tab 12 in this set. That is the document P257 and that is an Official Note, number 1187, from the Mirkovci police station. In the second paragraph of this Official Note it states: "The detainees were examined by the ambulance medical team headed by Gjorgi Karamanovski MD and some light injuries were established but the doctor said there was no need for any of the persons to be transferred to a health centre or a hospital." Tell me, Mr. Stojkov, when you see this document, during the examination, during your examining of the analytics documents in the OVR Cair, did you see this document maybe?

utterances.speaker: IGNO STOJKOV [Resumed]
utterances.text: As I said in my previous statements, all documents dated of the 12th - I'm talking about Official Notes - and a few days before the 12th, perhaps a week after, which were accessible to us at the moment, we looked at them, we read them, and we made copies of a majority of them.

utterances.speaker: MS. RESIDOVIC
utterances.text: Could you please look now at the document in tab 13. That is Exhibit P160. Again, it is submitted by Surlov Dragan. And I believe you stated yesterday that he was the person who told you that he was the duty officer on the 12th of August in Mirkovci police station. Tell me, do you remember when you are reading the contents of this note, do you feel that you had the opportunity to see this Official Note as well?

utterances.speaker: IGNO STOJKOV [Resumed]
utterances.text: This note, in view -- in particular that it is from police station Mirkovci, signed by my colleague Dragan, gives a chronological overview of events related to that day. Naturally, I am aware of this text, because I have read it, whether in this Official Note or in other individual notes about this event, I don't recall, but I am aware of this text.

utterances.speaker: MS. RESIDOVIC
utterances.text: I will kindly ask you now, Mr. Stojkov, to look at the document in tab 14. That is Exhibit P106, and that is a report signed by the chief of the OVR Cair on the 12th of August, 2001. In the last paragraph of this document, it is stated that the authorised officer of the Cair police station at 1545 brought the person Fetahovski Dilaver, born on 24th of April, 1981, from the village of Ljuboten, and his identification number is noted in this document: "In poor physical health, the individual was found on the street in the village of Radisani where he had been accosted by the locals. He was transferred to a Skopje city hospital by an ambulance car." Do you see it written here?

utterances.speaker: IGNO STOJKOV [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MS. RESIDOVIC
utterances.text: I will ask to you look at the document in tab 15. That is P157-- Exhibit P157. It is again a report from the OVR Cair, and please look now at the last paragraph in this report where it is stated: "During the interview they stated that they received at approximately 1330 hours a call for the transport of passengers from the settlement of Radisani towards Skopje after which they headed in the direction of Radisani. When they arrived at the last bus-stop of JSB 57, in the village of Radisani, they were accosted and stopped by a large group of citizens who threw themselves at them. They were pulled out and brought over to Cair police station owing to the swift intervention of authorised officials of Cair police station, while their motor vehicles were damaged by the citizens at the scene and were thereafter towed to the Cair police station for further procedure." First of all, let me ask you: Do you remember whether, when examining the documents in the analytics department, you saw this report or reports of similar contents?

utterances.speaker: IGNO STOJKOV [Resumed]
utterances.text: All reports from that period I saw them with my own eyes and I read them; and, as I said, a majority of them, we copied and took with us. This last paragraph which you read, when we asked about the police officers who took these people over in the police station, I knew that the police station should have taken further measures to establish whether the people have been injured, whether they're vehicles have been damaged and so forth. This is a regular task and obligation. It was not our current obligation at that moment. These are measures which they were due to undertake as police bodies.

utterances.speaker: MS. RESIDOVIC
utterances.text: Thank you for this clarification. I'm interested in another issue in relation to this both reports that we read because they both speak about the fact that citizens accosted and attacked villagers. If you had seen these documents, does this reflect your knowledge from that time and does it corroborate the information that you received from your colleagues from Cair about the events of that date?

utterances.speaker: IGNO STOJKOV [Resumed]
utterances.text: As I said yesterday, I could personally see that in front of the police station Cair and upwards towards the village of Radisani, there were a large number of persons, a lot of people, who had various objects in their hand, were yelling out various things. Most probably these people were upset by the events of the previous days. The small number of police officers, having in mind that -- that the police officers were also on various check-points and carried out their regular duties of patrolling and other regular daily tasks --

utterances.speaker: MS. RESIDOVIC
utterances.text: Very well. Thank you. In relation to this, tell me, when you spoke to the chief Krstevski, did he ever mention to you whether he personally or anyone else saw that the police took some measures outside of the scope of its responsibility, whether he had seen actually that the police was beating those villagers?

utterances.speaker: IGNO STOJKOV [Resumed]
utterances.text: In the discussions he told me, as I previously said, when we met he said that on that day, on the 12th of August, there was great movement; as he described it, chaos. There was a small number of police officers that were deployed and were carrying out their tasks, but in this concrete discussion the head Krstevski did not say that any of our colleagues used physical force unless this was absolutely necessary, unless they were attacked. However, he did not say that there was need to resort to physical force.

utterances.speaker: MS. RESIDOVIC
utterances.text: Very well. Thank you. Please look at the document after tab 16. This is Exhibit P154. And the question is simply: When you look at this document, tell me just do you remember this document and whether you had maybe seen or taken this document with you?

utterances.speaker: IGNO STOJKOV [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, I remember this document, because it's a report and, as I said, all reports from that period were read and were taken with us because in addition to giving a chronological overview on events, it provides a lot of information about people, their names and personal data, which was of concrete interest of us. I remember this document because weapons are mentioned, that weapons were brought into the police station Mirkovci.

utterances.speaker: MS. RESIDOVIC
utterances.text: Would you please look at the document after tab 17. And tell me, before you look at this report, you stated this several times already but I would like to ask you now if you are able to state more specifically. What were you looking for there? Were you investigating the events? Or were you trying to find something else in the documents that you were reviewing?

utterances.speaker: IGNO STOJKOV [Resumed]
utterances.text: Our tasks was not to chronologically compile these documents and bring them but to come to information that there were aggrieved or injured parties, whether by police forces, civilian forces or by the other side, the terrorists. We were looking for persons or, rather, reported injuries, injured persons, destroyed facilities.

utterances.speaker: MS. RESIDOVIC
utterances.text: Do you know when this situation calmed down and what actually happened to the citizens who -- villagers who started from the village of Ljuboten towards Skopje?

utterances.speaker: IGNO STOJKOV [Resumed]
utterances.text: I don't know personally what happened on that day because I was in Radisani and around the police station where I live. I don't know what happened on that day, but later, in my discussions with my colleagues, and from materials which I saw in police station Cair, I learned that enforcement was called in first, enforcements of police officers who arrived sometime in the afternoon and sometime during the evening the secure return of the population from the Ljuboten village was secured with, and I think this was done.

utterances.speaker: MS. RESIDOVIC
utterances.text: Thank you. I asked you now to look at the document behind tab 17. That is Exhibit P155. And since you just explained that you learned later and also through some of the documents that you reviewed, tell me please whether this is one of the documents that corroborates what you said about, when answering my previous question?

utterances.speaker: IGNO STOJKOV [Resumed]
utterances.text: I don't remember this document. It is possible that I have read it but perhaps I did not pay due attention and at that moment, perhaps it was not in the document, but I do not remember this document as such, but I know of this information.

utterances.speaker: MS. RESIDOVIC
utterances.text: Very well. Thank you. I will kindly ask you now to look at the document after tab 20. That is Exhibit P147. When discussing the issues at the OVR Cair or when reviewing the documents, have you seen a document indicating that, on that date, the identity of the MP Fatmir Etemi was established?

utterances.speaker: IGNO STOJKOV [Resumed]
utterances.text: I saw this Official Note then. I also know the text therein. The colleagues stopped the MP Etemi, a Member of Parliament at the time, and after they were brought in and interviewed, these people were set free.

utterances.speaker: MS. RESIDOVIC
utterances.text: Tell me, please, Mr. Stojkov, apart from the documents that we discussed yesterday, where there was information that on the 10th, on the date when the mine was planted under the army vehicle, people were seen, members of the NLA or maybe not members but armed individuals wearing black uniforms were seen entering the village. Did you notice any documents from which it could have been seen that those armed persons are still seen in the village?

utterances.speaker: IGNO STOJKOV [Resumed]
utterances.text: In the materials which we saw in police station Cair, as I already said, say that even before the 12th of August, people in black uniforms with arms were noted moving in and around the village. I think there were also documents after the event that there is still movement of armed persons dressed in black. It could not be established whether these were uniforms but it is said that they were dressed in black and that they are armed. I'm speaking now about after the 12th, perhaps this was the 14th, 15th, 13th ...

utterances.speaker: MS. RESIDOVIC
utterances.text: I will kindly ask you now to look first at the document after tab 21. That is 65 ter document number 299. This is a telegram that you testified about as having seen them but not having copied them. And then please look at the document after tab 22; that is the Exhibit P145. But let's focus first on the one after tab 21. The document bears the date 13th of August, 2001.

utterances.speaker: IGNO STOJKOV [Resumed]
utterances.text: This is a telegram which clarifies that relevant services are informed of the movement of persons in uniforms that have been noted.

utterances.speaker: MS. RESIDOVIC
utterances.text: I will ask you now to look at the document after tab 22. As I said, that is Exhibit P145, a document dated, again, 13th of August, 2001.

utterances.speaker: IGNO STOJKOV [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes. I know the text of this document, which is an Official Note. It comes after the telegram. I said already that we did not take telegrams with us. However, Official Notes which spoke of events after the 12th, we read most of them and we copied and took them with us.

utterances.speaker: MS. RESIDOVIC
utterances.text: Would you please have a look at the document after tab 23. That is 65 ter document 512. It is, again, a document, a report registered events and measures undertaken in connection with the operative action Ramno, dated 13th of August, 2001. And tell me, please, whether this document again corroborates what you stated before, that when reviewing the documents you actually saw that after the 12th, armed individuals were noticed in the village?

utterances.speaker: IGNO STOJKOV [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes. This document is information but information obtained from army positions which was sent to the police station, which then informed other bodies, or, rather, submitted a report of the measures that are to be taken. This is why I said that I know that in most of the documents which we checked, documents related to after the event, provided information that there was movement of armed persons in the area above Ljuboten.

utterances.speaker: MS. RESIDOVIC
utterances.text: [Previous translation continues] ... Say this document is an information received from the army positions. Is that so?

utterances.speaker: IGNO STOJKOV [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, from the army positions.

utterances.speaker: MS. RESIDOVIC
utterances.text: Would you please look at the document after tab 24. That is Exhibit P124. This document is probably one of those that you testified about, that were those on the basis of which you testified before this Court that you had seen documents speaking of presence of armed individuals in the village even after the 12th. Is that correct?

utterances.speaker: IGNO STOJKOV [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes. This is information from one of the police point from a military conscript given by name, that uniformed persons have been noted. Whether this report I read or copied, I cannot claim. But I said that there were certain documents which provide information that there is movement of armed persons.

utterances.speaker: MS. RESIDOVIC
utterances.text: And now, after having seen these documents dated on the 13th, your comment was that some of the information arrived from the army positions while others arrived from police check-points, so you had the information from both the army sources, received at the analytics as well as the police sources which were also found in the analytics department at the OVR Cair?

utterances.speaker: IGNO STOJKOV [Resumed]
utterances.text: In this period, the army of the Republic of Macedonia had its own positions. I don't know exactly where they were, but towards the border to Kosovo, above Ljuboten village. I don't exactly know where. The army had its own positions, the police had its own check-points on the main roads, streets, above the settlement of Radisani, towards the village of Ljubanci, towards the Ljuboten road. These are all places where the police had its check-points. The cooperation between army and police was carried out by way of information. The army informed the police of all the activities of the terrorists towards its own and I believe this was the same case vice versa; there must be some kind of coordination.

utterances.speaker: MS. RESIDOVIC
utterances.text: Very well. Thank you. Would you please look at the document after tab 25. That is an Official Note dated 13th of August, 2001, coming from the Mirkovci police station, Official Note number 11.91, subject is assistance provided to the emergency medical squad to transport a detained person to the city hospital. Considering the task that you had, as you explained it before this Court, would you please tell me whether you had seen this document and whether you had taken this document with you, if you had seen it?

utterances.speaker: IGNO STOJKOV [Resumed]
utterances.text: This is one of the basic documents which we looked at and took with us because this is -- it provides information on persons taken from the police station and taken to the city hospital.

utterances.speaker: MS. RESIDOVIC
utterances.text: Thank you. Would you please look now at the document after tab 26. That is Exhibit P259. This Official Note is, again, related to the same person that requested medical assistance and to whom this medical assistance was rendered. Was this a document that you had found and, given the nature of the task that you had, a document that you retained?

utterances.speaker: IGNO STOJKOV [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes. This is a follow-up information about previous request of approval from superiors in the duty centre for this person to be transferred into the city hospital. So I do know this document.

utterances.speaker: MS. RESIDOVIC
utterances.text: Would you please look now at the document after tab 27. That is Exhibit P400, Official Note number 1206. Again, submitted by Surlov Dragan, who informs that from the Mirkovci police station medical squad was called, ambulance car, and that the persons Adem Ametovski, Mevludin Bajrami, Nevaip Bajrami, and Ismail Ramadani were taken to the Skopje city hospital. Have you seen this document and is that a document that you remember as having copied for the performance of your task?

utterances.speaker: IGNO STOJKOV [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes. As I said previously, all documents that list information about persons which were in the police station - and here we have a situation also where medical assistance was requested for them - are documents which we read. This one I know I read and I made a copy of it, which I took with me.

utterances.speaker: MS. RESIDOVIC
utterances.text: Would you please now look at the document after tab 28. That is Official Note number 1209, and it is Exhibit P258. Do you remember, Mr. Stojkov, this document?

utterances.speaker: IGNO STOJKOV [Resumed]
utterances.text: I have most probably seen this document, but I think it is not part of the documents which I took with me because here it is only generally stated that medical assistance was called in regarding detained persons but it does not point to which persons and the reasons why the medical assistance was called in.

utterances.speaker: MS. RESIDOVIC
utterances.text: Would you please look now at the document after tab 30. That is Exhibit P54.045. Tell me, please, do you remember from that time having seen this document and, considering the task that you had, was it of relevance for you and did you copy that one as well?

utterances.speaker: IGNO STOJKOV [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes. As I said, we took this document because of the first part of the text contained therein. Previously, we knew that weapons had been brought in and seized. We were interested about information on the persons. I remember this document and I know that I took this -- a copy of this document with me.

utterances.speaker: MS. RESIDOVIC
utterances.text: Would you please now look at the next document after tab 31 and tell me - that is 65 ter 151 - tell me whether you treated this document in the same way as you explained with regards to the one before?

utterances.speaker: IGNO STOJKOV [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, the same applies. All documents which could contain any information with names of persons or personal data such as date of birth or where we could see that something was missing or is not just right, we made copies of this and we took it with us.

utterances.speaker: MS. RESIDOVIC
utterances.text: Before asking you some questions of general nature related to several documents, I will ask you to please just look at the document after tab 32. That is Exhibit P261 and that is an Official Note, number 537, submitted by Blagoja Toskovski. And subject is report on a deceased person.

utterances.speaker: IGNO STOJKOV [Resumed]
utterances.text: I know this note, because it deals with a person which had previously been taken by the emergency ambulance and taken to the city hospital. Since this is an information stating that the person deceased in the hospital, this is one of the documents which we took with us.

utterances.speaker: MS. RESIDOVIC
utterances.text: Mr. Stojkov, a number of documents before as well as this document indicated that several persons were taken to a hospital and that one of them died. Yesterday you spoke to us about an event involving a three-year-old girl and her father and you state that you had went to the hospital. Why did you go then to the hospital? What was the purpose of your visit there?

utterances.speaker: IGNO STOJKOV [Resumed]
utterances.text: I went -- I was the only one from my working group who went to the hospital together with two persons from police forensics. The goal was to document this case… of course, we wanted to have a photograph of the girl in order to establish the circumstances. I took my colleagues from forensics to photograph this girl and to pick up the bullet which was taken from him [as interpreted], which needed to be further processed. I was also there to show them which vehicle needed to be processed from a forensic point of view, and I went to see the girl in view of the fact that this was a three-year-old girl and --

utterances.speaker: MS. RESIDOVIC
utterances.text: Very well. When the issue was about the three-year-old girl, you went to hospital. When you saw this document, this report about the death of Atulla Qaili, did you go to the hospital?

utterances.speaker: IGNO STOJKOV [Resumed]
utterances.text: We did not go to hospital because the information was that death occurred on the 13th of August. The set-up of the working group and taking over of the Ljuboten case came six months later. Regardless, though, our job was not to collect medical information from the hospital. There were other services charged with that task, most frequently, medical documents were received from aggrieved injured parties after their kidnapping, for example, or after they were set free, or, in the case of people deceased, these were documents received from their families or from relevant services. Therefore, we did not go to the hospital in order to investigate or to document a case.

utterances.speaker: MS. RESIDOVIC
utterances.text: Mr. Stojkov, you stated now: We were not investigating the events, that was a task or other services were charged with that. Could you please explain it more precisely? For instance, if this was happening in Cair what were the bodies that needed to investigate that event if such event took place within the territory they covered?

utterances.speaker: IGNO STOJKOV [Resumed]
utterances.text: Generally speaking, in the case of a homicide, the body in charge is that where -- located on the territory where this act was committed. Whenever a death occurs, an internal affairs body is informed or the police station which then informs the duty centre, gives information by way of telephone first, and then the duty centre reports this to the public prosecutor's office and the investigating judge. Then the police station, on the territory of which the crime was committed or where death occurred, it could be not only by way of murder, also by an accident, then engage homicide inspectors and police forensics.

utterances.speaker: MS. RESIDOVIC
utterances.text: So if I understood properly what you have just stated, your working group was not tasked with taking over the duties of bodies that are tasked with such competences by the law. Have I understood you properly?

utterances.speaker: IGNO STOJKOV [Resumed]
utterances.text: We were not authorised, not -- nor skilled to investigate the cause of death of any individual. Our task was to obtain basic documents that will point out to what happened. Once we documented a case, i.e., we gathered all the documents, or as I stated yesterday, once we received all the written documents, be they records of on-site investigations, photographs, forensic or other material, and, if it was possible for us, we found someone from the injured parties or their family members, we would establish contact if that was possible given the fact that on many occasions we were unable to establish contact and even if we did we were turned down, and it was then that we would officially interview the person. This is the procedure we followed.

utterances.speaker: MS. RESIDOVIC
utterances.text: Very well Mr. Stojkov, I understand this. You did not go to the hospital because that person has already died and those injured persons were probably not in the hospital any longer after six months. But tell me please after you had read this Official Note that some person that was previously at the police station was then taken to a hospital and then died, did you raise this issue with your colleagues at the OVR Cair when you saw this document? Did you ask them whether they did what you are now saying that they should have, whether they informed someone?

utterances.speaker: IGNO STOJKOV [Resumed]
utterances.text: [Previous translation continues] ... Person was taken from police station Mirkovci. We talked to some of our colleagues who did not want to speak on the record, and this was their right; I could not force them to talk to me. We were interested in what exactly happened. There's official information about the death of the person, so we were interested to know whether measures that needed to be taken were taken. As far as I understood, they said they informed the duty centre, the public prosecutor's office. Once this is done, the obligation fall upon other bodies.

utterances.speaker: MS. RESIDOVIC
utterances.text: Very well. Thank you. Maybe we should take a note that this is an Official Note number 537. And now I would like to ask to you to look at the document after tab 33. Considering your previous evidence, I do not expect that this was a topic of your interest, but I will ask you again -- and that is Exhibit P46.16. So I'm asking you whether you saw this document and whether you remembered it?

utterances.speaker: IGNO STOJKOV [Resumed]
utterances.text: To be honest, this is information for the basic public prosecutor's office. I don't remember whether I saw it or not. But it does mention Official Note, which I think we saw previously, which informs about a deceased person. This is information to the basic public prosecution office. At the moment when I was looking at it, I was probably thinking that this was not of interest to our working group, because this is information to the basic public prosecutor's office about a deceased person.

utterances.speaker: MS. RESIDOVIC
utterances.text: Thank you. So, you can agree with me that from the moment that the Official Note was produced on the 14th of August, when the police received the information about the death, if this is the date of sending the information to the OJO -- what does OJO stand for, can you please tell me what it stands for, OJO Skopje?

utterances.speaker: IGNO STOJKOV [Resumed]
utterances.text: Basic public prosecutor's office.

utterances.speaker: MS. RESIDOVIC
utterances.text: So on that same date that information was forwarded by the police to the basic public prosecutor's office. Is that correct?

utterances.speaker: IGNO STOJKOV [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes. According to this document, it is immediately reported to the basic public prosecutor's office. The previous note informs of the death of this person, according to the dates, it follows that information to the public prosecutor's office was sent immediately.

utterances.speaker: MS. RESIDOVIC
utterances.text: Since you stated some general affairs within the realm of your knowledge, could you tell me what does the police do when they inform the public prosecutor and the investigating judge? Whose orders does it take in order to take any further actions?

utterances.speaker: IGNO STOJKOV [Resumed]
utterances.text: Generally speaking, after a crime or event is reported to the public prosecutor's office, all police measures are also reported taking before and after the event; and after the public prosecutor's office is informed police bodies are put at the disposal of the public prosecutor's office.

utterances.speaker: MS. RESIDOVIC
utterances.text: Thank you. Could you please look now at the document after tab 34. That is Exhibit number 1D69, and that is an Official Note that -- that states that the inspection team at the SVR Skopje, police forensics department, took papillary lines of unknown deceased person from the mortuary in Butel in order to establish the identity of such person. Considering what you stated before, does it mean that the police reacted after it was requested to take some action?

utterances.speaker: IGNO STOJKOV [Resumed]
utterances.text: This has most probably been done at the request of the investigating judge or the basic public prosecutor's office. Some -- someone from the forensics unit wanted to establish the identity of this person. Most probably this was done at the request of the investigating judge.

utterances.speaker: MS. RESIDOVIC
utterances.text: The document itself does not state that such request came from the investigating judge or the public prosecutor. So, on the basis of what you do you draw that conclusions that it was most probably done upon the request of an investigating judge?

utterances.speaker: IGNO STOJKOV [Resumed]
utterances.text: In cases such as this, when the identity of the person is unknown, and the public prosecution and surely the investigating judge also, it is -- it is natural that these measures have been taken. As I said, after these two bodies have been informed, then police undertakes measures which are requested by these two bodies.

utterances.speaker: MS. RESIDOVIC
utterances.text: Thank you. If you remember, the information sent to the public prosecutor's office was sent on the 14th of August. This document bears the date 20th of August. So does this fact corroborate again that your surmise is right, that this was done after the body was informed?

utterances.speaker: IGNO STOJKOV [Resumed]
utterances.text: If we look at the date, the 14th, it was preceded with information to the prosecution and probably the investigating judge. Therefore, this is a request surely from the investigating judge to establish the identity of this person.

utterances.speaker: MS. RESIDOVIC
utterances.text: Thank you. Would you now please look at the document after tab 38. That is Exhibit P490 and that is a report, and as far as I understood, you stated that you copied almost all reports from that time and took them with you. Tell me, please, do you remember this report?

utterances.speaker: IGNO STOJKOV [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, I remember this report, because, as we can see, there are handwritten notes and there have been some changes made to it.

utterances.speaker: MS. RESIDOVIC
utterances.text: This report speaks of some other activities that took place on the 14th. Tell me, please, does this report reflect what you heard from the chief Krstevski, that on that date, it was not possible for the inspection team, on-site investigation team, to enter the village?

utterances.speaker: IGNO STOJKOV [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes. In my discussions with Chief Krstevski, I was informed that two attempts were made to enter the village after -- the day after the event, after the 12th of August, teams of police forensics and investigating judges, medical teams, forensic medicine were set up in order to go into the village, in view of the information that persons will be buried or have been buried. I cannot tell you precisely at this moment.

utterances.speaker: MS. RESIDOVIC
utterances.text: Would you please now look at the document after tab 40. That is Exhibit P149. And that is operational information, bearing the number 540, from the 15th of August. My first question is: Do you remember from that time, having seen this document?

utterances.speaker: IGNO STOJKOV [Resumed]
utterances.text: I don't remember having seen this document, but it was interesting that in that period there were several pieces of information that the persons of Albanian ethnicity who were deceased were not reported. Their death was not reported, and that they still figure as living in the records. That was interesting. But I have not seen this report with my own eyes.

utterances.speaker: MS. RESIDOVIC
utterances.text: Considering that the task of your group was to follow the traces of the injured or aggrieved parties and to find out what was done with regards to them, whether it was torture, ill-treatment, or property damage to the aggrieved parties, would you please tell me now whether what you heard about the practice that the Albanian population failed to report the deaths, did it have any influence on the work of your working group?

utterances.speaker: IGNO STOJKOV [Resumed]
utterances.text: As I said previously, contacts with persons, be it from Macedonian or Albanian or other ethnicity, were difficult to establish. There was lack of trust among every one of them. It was even difficult to find some persons. We had some information about them, but when we tried to reach them, they were either away, abroad, they were not there, perhaps some of them were even dead, but we did not have concrete information to that end.

utterances.speaker: MS. RESIDOVIC
utterances.text: I will kindly ask you to look now at the document after tab 42. That is 65 ter 476. Tell me, please, do you remember this document?

utterances.speaker: IGNO STOJKOV [Resumed]
utterances.text: According to the date, I can see that this document -- I don't remember this document, but I know that there were still attacks from armed persons towards police points and army positions towards civilian houses.

utterances.speaker: MS. RESIDOVIC
utterances.text: If a house was set on fire, would you have been interested in that as well?

utterances.speaker: IGNO STOJKOV [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes. Among the other cases which we worked on, we worked also on houses, civilian houses, religious facilities, factories, state facilities, and all damages incurred to them on any basis.

utterances.speaker: MS. RESIDOVIC
utterances.text: And when reviewing the documents in the analytics of OVR Cair were you able to find such materials stating that after that event, houses in the village were set on fire?

utterances.speaker: IGNO STOJKOV [Resumed]
utterances.text: All the materials well dealt with damage to facilities of any kind, we surely looked at. But unless there was a report from the owner, from the injured party, we would not take any measures, because, as I said, the procedure was to report this to the police station. If we speak about a house set on fire, then surely we investigated this and we created a file on this event.

utterances.speaker: MS. RESIDOVIC
utterances.text: Very well. Thank you. Would you now please look at the document after tab 44. That is Exhibit P135. Tell me, please, whether you remember this document or maybe this is something that you did not remember, when reviewing the documents at the OVR Cair?

utterances.speaker: IGNO STOJKOV [Resumed]
utterances.text: The document states what I said earlier about an information about houses in the village set on fire, but there are no such reports in the police station. Therefore, I know this as information, I know it, I've read it, I have seen it. However, I could not have undertaken measures because they were not reported in the police station.

utterances.speaker: MS. RESIDOVIC
utterances.text: Would you please now look at the document after tab 45. That is Exhibit P50.010. Do you remember having seen this information?

utterances.speaker: IGNO STOJKOV [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, I remember, because this is a collection of -- of a chronological overview of all events from 10th to 13th, and they were -- there are a lot of information contained therein. I know that I made copy of this information and that I took it with me.

utterances.speaker: MS. RESIDOVIC
utterances.text: Thank you. You testified yesterday that in the conversations with your colleagues or with the chief of the OVR Cair you heard that it was difficult for them to establish anything, because the villagers from Ljuboten did not want to contact the police. Do you remember that you spoke about that?

utterances.speaker: IGNO STOJKOV [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, I remember. I know there were some contacts even with some persons from the village, but when more concrete information was requested or when statements were requested, these same persons, due to pressure or other reasons, did not want to contact or to have contacts with police bodies.

utterances.speaker: MS. RESIDOVIC
utterances.text: You stated that you were reviewing those numerous documents pertaining to the month of August because you were mainly interested in the events in and around the village of Ljuboten so that you could see whether there were aggrieved parties and whether you could obtain some information about them. I would like to ask you now to look at the document after tab 48. That is a document that is Exhibit P104, and it was produced on the 15th of November, 2001. Or the 16th of November. I believe that this would be the correct date, although in the English translation, 15th November is noted, but it is not really that important. Would you please now look at this document, whether the contents of this document correspond to what you testified about. Is that what your colleagues were speaking about or is it related to some different situation?

utterances.speaker: IGNO STOJKOV [Resumed]
utterances.text: I have not seen this document in the course of my work, but according to the text, which I can see now, it is not to be excluded that this is about a contact from the village board with the aim of obtaining some more concrete information from him. As I can see, this person first agreed to help and assist the work of the police but then later did not want to provide any help or any information.

utterances.speaker: MS. RESIDOVIC
utterances.text: Thank you very much. Mr. Stojkov, when you made copies of the documents that you were interested in and those who were able to provide you with information related to the task of your group, to reach the aggrieved parties and their families so that they could give you some information about the event, tell me, please, what did you with those documents once you came back to your office?

utterances.speaker: IGNO STOJKOV [Resumed]
utterances.text: Since we had copies of the documents, we made case files in two copies; therefore, immediately we made yet another copy of these documents and we put it next to our case files. We had a short working meeting about what we should be doing next, what should we do as a follow-up to the information that we had gathered. This is the regular procedure.

utterances.speaker: MS. RESIDOVIC
utterances.text: Considering that you had not received any information from your colleagues at Cair on how to contact any aggrieved parties because they told you that they were unwilling to talk to them, would you tell me now what did you do in your group? Did you give up or were you still willing to do something?

utterances.speaker: IGNO STOJKOV [Resumed]
utterances.text: We talked about this and we saw that quite some time had elapsed from the event and that there were no reports on any injured persons. Our colleagues from the police station in OVR Cair tried but did not establish contacts with persons. So we, among us, agreed, through our contacts to try to get in touch with someone from the village who could help us find the persons listed in the documents.

utterances.speaker: MS. RESIDOVIC
utterances.text: And did you succeed in that, in establishing contact with someone from the village or with some of the aggrieved persons?

utterances.speaker: IGNO STOJKOV [Resumed]
utterances.text: To be quite honest, I had some contacts with some persons from the village. I have -- I maintained these contacts with these persons who were then and are still now my friends. But there was no possibility for these persons to help us in any way, because, as I said yesterday, both Macedonians and Albanians were afraid of everything that was happening at that time.

utterances.speaker: MS. RESIDOVIC
utterances.text: Considering that explaining your method of work, you stated that, in addition to collecting these written materials and writing some Official Note about any interviews with the aggrieved persons and their families, what was then the method that you used in this case?

utterances.speaker: IGNO STOJKOV [Resumed]
utterances.text: The methodology of our working group entails that, after the return from the site, or after an interview, or something is noted, an Official Note is made on what has been done in those few days. In the Ljuboten case, the case file of Ljuboten includes our visit to the police station Mirkovci and Cair. An Official Note was made stating that on those particular days we were there, that we established contacts with the chiefs and all of these materials are put in the case file. This is the regular practice.

utterances.speaker: MS. RESIDOVIC
utterances.text: Considering that not even your personal contacts and efforts to arrive at some information or more details, whether those persons whose names you found there were really victims or not, tell me, please, what you did later about that case. Was something done at all about it, and what was that period of time when you reached the conclusion that you were unable to get any further information?

utterances.speaker: IGNO STOJKOV [Resumed]
utterances.text: As I said, the case was put next to the other case files with a note in our log-books that we should continue to try to find some of the aggrieved persons. I know that in that period, I believe Katica Jovanovska from analytics also was preparing some information about the event in Ljuboten. There is a possibility that some of these materials or copies of the materials were also left with her for further processing. Other measures were not taken because the public was already being informed that there was going to be exhumation of the persons in Ljuboten and that police were -- forensics were going to work on this. So we left it at that, to wait for the exhumation, to see the report of the expertise, and then to continue working.

utterances.speaker: MS. RESIDOVIC
utterances.text: Did you, the working group and you yourself, at that time, when you concluded that you needed to wait for the results that could provide additional indicators or additional possibilities for investigation, so did you ever discuss the results of your work -- work on this case, on other previous cases, did you discuss it in any meetings, and, in particular, was there any communication with the public prosecutor's office?

utterances.speaker: IGNO STOJKOV [Resumed]
utterances.text: There were several meetings. On one of the bigger meetings where Mr. Apostol Stojanovski and I were called was at the office of the director at the time, Mr. Goran Mitevski. Others present there were a colleague from forensics - I don't remember his name; Katica Jovanovska. Mr. Stavre Dzikov, public prosecutor general at the time; and Mr. Jordan Arsov. This was a working meeting which we were called to attend with a view of finalising the work in progress. We came to this meeting with a lot of materials, other materials were also brought in, most -- and we were discussing about the collection of these materials, processing of these materials, and what needs to be done before they're handed over to the public prosecution. Whether criminal charges and reports were needed by-- to be prepared by the police and so forth. This was a working meeting and we were discussing our work.

utterances.speaker: MS. RESIDOVIC
utterances.text: Was that the only meeting that you attended?

utterances.speaker: IGNO STOJKOV [Resumed]
utterances.text: I attended several meetings, but if I understood your question correctly, you were asking about meetings with the public prosecutor. I attended other meetings, but in terms of meetings with the public prosecution, in addition to this one where Stavre Dzikov attended, we had an additional meeting with our colleagues from the public prosecutor's office. Myself, Mr. Goran Mitevski, Mr. Apostol Stojanovski, and Mr. Uslinkovski from police forensics attended this meeting and two other colleagues from the public prosecutor's office whose name escapes me at the moment. I know that near the end of the meeting -- this was a lengthy meeting and we were discussing a lot of the material, each case was being looked into and we tried to coordinate our efforts. I remember that Ms. Sofija Galeva entered near the end of the meeting, this is the first time I met her and I learned that she was working at the office of the minister. She was also interested in our materials. I cannot remember whether she too was working on some of this, but she sat down for a short while. They were talking with the director, Goran Mitevski, and some people from forensics about these materials.

utterances.speaker: MS. RESIDOVIC
utterances.text: If I understood you well yesterday, when you finished, when you thought that you done everything that you could, that you had gathered all the documents that you were able to gather, you then made a list, submitted that list with the analytics and then the analytics forwarded this to the body that was in charge of producing the criminal report. Tell me, please, with regards to this Ljuboten case, did you develop this in the same way, and was it also processed using the same method used by your working group?

utterances.speaker: IGNO STOJKOV [Resumed]
utterances.text: Our practice was the following: Once a case, a case file is sufficiently processed according to our view, that is to say that we had gathered enough material in order to prepare a criminal report, we sent this material with a note. Two copies of this were sent to the analytics department, which processed this material analytically and then forwarded one copy to the public prosecutor's office or relevant bodies, police stations or OVRs, who prepared the criminal report, which they then forward to the public prosecutor's office where it is turned into an indictment. We had many unfinished cases among which -- including the Ljuboten file. To this day, I see this as an unfinished file. I told you the reasons for this. I told you why this was so. We were not able to establish contact with aggrieved persons and there were no persons who reported anything. There were no injured persons. Therefore, things were left as they were. The exhumation then followed, and when this was done, we were not allowed to look at these documents; I don't know the reasons for this. And afterwards, the working group stopped working and was disbanded at the beginning of 2003.

utterances.speaker: MS. RESIDOVIC
utterances.text: Thank you very much, Mr. Stojkov.

utterances.speaker: MS. RESIDOVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Your Honour, I have concluded my examination of this witness.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE PARKER
utterances.text: Thank you very much, Ms. Residovic. We will have our first break now and resume at 4.00.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE PARKER
utterances.text: Ms. Residovic.

utterances.speaker: MS. RESIDOVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Your Honours, I seek to tender three documents as Defence exhibit, documents that I showed to the witness. I had a discussion during the break with my learned colleague the Prosecutor and as far as I understood, he would not object. Those documents are 65 ter 299; that is in tab 21. Then 65 ter document 512; in tab 23. And 65 ter document 476; in tab 42.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE PARKER
utterances.text: There's no objection, Mr. Dobbyn.

utterances.speaker: MR. DOBBYN
utterances.text: No, there's not, Your Honours.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE PARKER
utterances.text: Thank you. Those three documents will each separately be received.

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: Your Honours, 65 ter 299 will become Exhibit 1D288. 65 ter 512 will become Exhibit 1D289. And 65 ter 476 will become Exhibit 1D290.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE PARKER
utterances.text: Thank you. Mr. Apostolski, are there any questions of this witness?

utterances.speaker: MR. APOSTOLSKI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Good afternoon, Your Honours. The Defence of Johan Tarculovski has no questions for this witness.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE PARKER
utterances.text: Thank you very much. Mr. Dobbyn.

utterances.speaker: MR. DOBBYN
utterances.text: Good afternoon, Your Honours.

utterances.speaker: MR. DOBBYN
utterances.text: And good afternoon, Mr. Stojkov. My name is Gerard Dobbyn and I'm representing the Office of the Prosecutor here. So following on from my colleague Ms. Residovic I will be asking you some questions about the matters that you have testified to so far.

utterances.speaker: MR. DOBBYN
utterances.text: And perhaps before we start, I do have some binders that we prepared for this witness and this might be the best time to distribute those.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE PARKER
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MR. DOBBYN
utterances.text: And, Mr. Stojkov, I understand from your testimony that you started working for the Ministry of Interior in 1991. Is that correct?

utterances.speaker: IGNO STOJKOV [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, this is correct.

utterances.speaker: MR. DOBBYN
utterances.text: And from what you've said it appears that you have made some pretty steady progress in your career. You started as an intern in 1991, and you have the position that you do today. So would you agree that you appear to have progressed quite smoothly throughout the Ministry of Interior?

utterances.speaker: IGNO STOJKOV [Resumed]
utterances.text: In the 16 and a half, 17 years that I have been in the service, it is quite natural to go through the process of going from the lower positions up the scale to higher positions.

utterances.speaker: MR. DOBBYN
utterances.text: And prior to joining the military crimes working group in 2001, you already had extensive investigative experience, didn't you?

utterances.speaker: IGNO STOJKOV [Resumed]
utterances.text: As inspector, yes, in the operative segments.

utterances.speaker: MR. DOBBYN
utterances.text: And you also testified to having had extensive specialised training and courses that were run by other national police forces. Isn't that correct?

utterances.speaker: IGNO STOJKOV [Resumed]
utterances.text: This is correct. My training starts after some years of working at the Ministry of Interior. The first training was in June 1999. I started my employment in 1991. This means that I had to go through certain parts of police work in order to get to a position where I should get training for other areas.

utterances.speaker: MR. DOBBYN
utterances.text: And in that training, I believe you described attending courses in Germany and Britain, in the US and France and in Egypt. Is that right?

utterances.speaker: IGNO STOJKOV [Resumed]
utterances.text: Except in Cairo, Egypt, there were also trainings in the Republic of Macedonia.

utterances.speaker: MR. DOBBYN
utterances.text: And some of the areas covered in these training courses included investigating illicit drug trafficking, weapons of mass destruction, radioactive weapons, and terrorism. Have I left anything out of that list?

utterances.speaker: IGNO STOJKOV [Resumed]
utterances.text: …some of the training courses included checking traffic and uncovering illicit drugs and weapons trafficking. And, in addition to this, the training in Egypt which was against terrorist actions.

utterances.speaker: MR. DOBBYN
utterances.text: When you attended these training courses, did you take this training seriously?

utterances.speaker: IGNO STOJKOV [Resumed]
utterances.text: I think I have a serious approach to my work. Since this was specialisation training which I need in the course of my work, I believe that I gave my maximum in these specialised trainings.

utterances.speaker: MR. DOBBYN
utterances.text: So you're saying you worked hard at this training. Would it be fair to say that you picked up a lot of knowledge and a lot of skill from these trainings?

utterances.speaker: IGNO STOJKOV [Resumed]
utterances.text: What was requested of me by the training officers was performed by me to the maximum extent possible.

utterances.speaker: MR. DOBBYN
utterances.text: Do you feel that you learned a lot of knowledge and skills from these training programmes?

utterances.speaker: IGNO STOJKOV [Resumed]
utterances.text: I don't want to speak about my own qualifications. This should be shown in my work. It should be said by my superiors and by my colleagues who work with me. I believe that I carry out my work in a professional and concrete manner and I put in maximum efforts in order to get things done.

utterances.speaker: MR. DOBBYN
utterances.text: Okay. And in the course of your career, and, again, through these training courses, do you think you've learned to think critically about matters?

utterances.speaker: IGNO STOJKOV [Resumed]
utterances.text: Everyone who is involved in police work, unless one is critical and is able to be self-critical also and see one's own mistake, cannot carry out his work well.

utterances.speaker: MR. DOBBYN
utterances.text: And would you agree that one would also not carry out his work well if one did not look at all possibilities, at all different angles, in an investigation?

utterances.speaker: IGNO STOJKOV [Resumed]
utterances.text: If we are talking about a criminal act, an investigation includes the police bodies and other organs which investigate this crime. By rule and in practice each one should do its part of the work, which means the responsible in investigating the crime must look into all aspects of this investigation in order for it to be completed successfully.

utterances.speaker: MR. DOBBYN
utterances.text: So would you agree it's important not to just take something at face value but to really dig in and look at all different possibilities in a situation?

utterances.speaker: IGNO STOJKOV [Resumed]
utterances.text: In principle, nothing should be taken at face value. However, there are situations where we, as inspectors, or employees of the ministry working on concrete cases, must take into consideration even the most insignificant piece of information, because this can lead us to some sort of trace that will help us work on this case.

utterances.speaker: MR. DOBBYN
utterances.text: So you would agree that would be very important when doing your work, Mr. Stojkov. And when I was speaking to you just a few moments ago I asked you about your on view of your own talents and abilities and you said that you would prefer to be judged by your peers, by your colleagues. Do you remember that?

utterances.speaker: IGNO STOJKOV [Resumed]
utterances.text: Of course.

utterances.speaker: MR. DOBBYN
utterances.text: And, in fact, throughout your career, you have received recognition for the quality of your work, haven't you?

utterances.speaker: IGNO STOJKOV [Resumed]
utterances.text: I don't know what kind of recognition you are talking about, but what I can say, that in the course of my career, and this is something I said some -- I said yesterday, that I had been often awarded and recognised for my work.

utterances.speaker: MR. DOBBYN
utterances.text: And as an example, isn't it correct that in 2000, you were rewarded with a pistol?

utterances.speaker: IGNO STOJKOV [Resumed]
utterances.text: Correct. In 2000, on the proposal of my superiors at the time, and in view of the fact that I had already been employed for ten years in the Ministry of Interior and this is kind of a jubilee or an anniversary, my superiors recommended to the commission which was, at that time, at the office of the minister, and this recommendation was approved by the said commission, and thus I received a pistol.

utterances.speaker: MR. DOBBYN
utterances.text: And you have also been rewarded financially on several occasions, haven't you?

utterances.speaker: IGNO STOJKOV [Resumed]
utterances.text: It is customary not only in the Macedonian police, I see this as the case in other police forces in other countries, that it is customary that one be recommended for financial awards once a difficult case is finished.

utterances.speaker: MR. DOBBYN
utterances.text: And, in fact, you were once awarded with an increase of 15 per cent of your salary for achieving extraordinary results in your work with the military crimes working group. Isn't that right?

utterances.speaker: IGNO STOJKOV [Resumed]
utterances.text: I cannot recall because I have been awarded several times with a 15 per cent increase of my monthly salary at the ministry. There is a possibility that I was awarded also as part of this working group. I cannot remember at this moment.

utterances.speaker: MR. DOBBYN
utterances.text: Well, perhaps if you could turn to tab 1 of the binder in front of you. And this document is 65 ter number 1149. And if you could turn to what would be the third page in the English translation, and I believe would be the fifth page in Macedonian, you'll see a document dated 4th of October, 2001. Do you see the document I'm talking about?

utterances.speaker: IGNO STOJKOV [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. DOBBYN
utterances.text: And approximately halfway down the page you'll see a title: Elaboration. Do you see that?

utterances.speaker: IGNO STOJKOV [Resumed]
utterances.text: Please repeat it.

utterances.speaker: MR. DOBBYN
utterances.text: There should be a title halfway down the page stating, Elaboration, and under that the first line would be starting: The named person in September 2001.

utterances.speaker: IGNO STOJKOV [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, I see it.

utterances.speaker: MR. DOBBYN
utterances.text: So just to read that to you it says: "The named person, in September 2001, has achieved extraordinary results, respectively, has performed the duties with a remarkable success and quality. Respectively, the given tasks in the sphere of the working group for gathering evidences for committed war crimes on the territory of the Republic of Macedonia are finished in due time and with quality which contributes for a successful accomplishment of the basic function of the working group and gathering of quality evidences." Do you see that?

utterances.speaker: IGNO STOJKOV [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. DOBBYN
utterances.text: So this raise was given to you for the quality of your work with the working group. Correct?

utterances.speaker: IGNO STOJKOV [Resumed]
utterances.text: This is what is written here, so it must be for this.

utterances.speaker: MR. DOBBYN
utterances.text: And, Mr. Stojkov, you've talked about putting in full effort in your work and does that include being very thorough in your work?

utterances.speaker: IGNO STOJKOV [Resumed]
utterances.text: As I said, I think I respond to all tasks then and now and in the course of all of my work with the utmost seriousness. There are things or documents which can -- or persons which cannot be got to at the moment. However, I tried to put in my best effort.

utterances.speaker: MR. DOBBYN
utterances.text: And as an investigator, do you recognise that it is very important to keep thorough and accurate records of investigations?

utterances.speaker: IGNO STOJKOV [Resumed]
utterances.text: In the course of investigations led by an inspector, first, notes are taken in a daily log-book. Each one has a note pad where tasks and obligations carried out are listed. As a rule, after certain information has been obtained or interviewed had been carried out or on-site investigation has been carried out, an Official Note has to be prepared. A written document about the activities carried out. It may be several activities in the course of one day, which means several written documents; or it may be one Official Note covering several days, which explain the activities and measures taken by the inspector in that period of time.

utterances.speaker: MR. DOBBYN
utterances.text: So if I understand you correctly, you're agreeing that it is important to take notes and in fact in your practice you would take notes of all tasks that were undertaken in an investigation. Is that correct?

utterances.speaker: IGNO STOJKOV [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes. I took notes in my note pads. These are my personal pads where I took notes. To this day, I have notes of my work, I take information from people and so forth. This is one of my basic tasks.

utterances.speaker: MR. DOBBYN
utterances.text: Thank you. And I'd like to now move on ask you some questions specifically about the working group on military crimes. And you testified that this working group for gathering evidence on military crimes was formed in May 2001. Do you know why there was a need to establish such a working group?

utterances.speaker: IGNO STOJKOV [Resumed]
utterances.text: I stated that later, when I joined the working group, that is, I learned there was the initial working group that was established in May 2001. That group had the same tasks as us certainly, to see whether there were any grounds to believe that some crimes, war crimes were committed. I'm sure that this was why that working group was established.

utterances.speaker: MR. DOBBYN
utterances.text: Specifically, why was this working group established in 2001?

utterances.speaker: IGNO STOJKOV [Resumed]
utterances.text: Since specifically, in 2001, in January or February I believe, the Republic of Macedonia became involved in the so-called military conflict. So, as a consequence of this, there was a need to establish such working group.

utterances.speaker: MR. DOBBYN
utterances.text: And what did you understand the term "military crimes" to mean?

utterances.speaker: IGNO STOJKOV [Resumed]
utterances.text: I think, so I'm saying about me personally, I'm not qualified to give you a general meaning of that notion. But for me, anything that is classified as war crime and that has been perpetrated during that time of military conflict and perpetrated by uniformed individuals should be categorised as war crimes.

utterances.speaker: MR. DOBBYN
utterances.text: And just to summarize again I believe you testified that --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE PARKER
utterances.text: Ms. Residovic.

utterances.speaker: MS. RESIDOVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Your Honour, I apologise for interrupting my colleague, but obviously that notion is interpreted wrongly. In the text of the decision, it is stated war crimes, no military crimes are related, so I suggest that the term is used as used in the document when this working group is discussed.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE PARKER
utterances.text: I think you may find that the term is used variously in different documents. Two decisions of the minister, your client, for example, in one there is a reference to war crimes; in another there's reference to a different description.

utterances.speaker: MS. RESIDOVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Yes. But in the Macedonian, it says "voeni zlostorstva" which would be war crimes. As it is also used in numerous documents, speaking about this working group. I'm not a linguist but I'm indicating that such problem exists. In Macedonian, that is war crimes.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE PARKER
utterances.text: For example, in your tab 1, the order of the -- of the previous witness -- no, of this present witness, the decision is translated in English as "military crimes" --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE PARKER
utterances.text: -- whereas in the document at tab 2, dated the 9th of October, 2001, in paragraph 1, the meaning -- the words are translated as "war crimes" in English.

utterances.speaker: MS. RESIDOVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Your Honours, I apologise, really, neither my English nor my Macedonian are so good that I could really speak about it, but "vojna" in my language, in Bosnian, means "military"; but in Macedonian "voena" means "war". So possibility in the course of translation , it is not us translating those documents, such confusion occurs between the B/C/S version and the Macedonian version. So perhaps it would be best if the witness could say what "Vojna" means in Macedonian, so then we could also correct the other documents simultaneously. Thank you very much, and I apologise again.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE PARKER
utterances.text: Any correction will be on the basis of an authorised translation, rather than the witness's understanding, and at the moment, the authorised translations give us two different concepts. So if either you or Mr. Dobbyn want to pursue that with the translation authorities, you may do so. But at the moment we have two different concepts. Whether they mean something different is yet another question. Mr. Dobbyn.

utterances.speaker: MR. DOBBYN
utterances.text: Thank you, Your Honours.

utterances.speaker: MR. DOBBYN
utterances.text: Now, just to go back, Mr. Stojkov, I believe you testified that you started assisting the working group in September 2001, and you became a permanent member in October of that year. Is that right?

utterances.speaker: IGNO STOJKOV [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, that is correct.

utterances.speaker: MR. DOBBYN
utterances.text: And you were a member of the working group until February 2003. Does that sound correct to you?

utterances.speaker: IGNO STOJKOV [Resumed]
utterances.text: I know that it was towards the beginning of 2003. Probably it is correct that it was in February of 2003.

utterances.speaker: MR. DOBBYN
utterances.text: And when you stopped working as a member of the working group, was that because the work of that group was finished, or did you move on to another position while they continued their work?

utterances.speaker: IGNO STOJKOV [Resumed]
utterances.text: We stopped working as a working group practically because we were appointed through a minister's decision. So we never actually stopped working the working group, I mean, because we never received a document stating that our involvement in the working group finishes. During that period, somewhere before the new year, I don't remember precisely, the political party in power changed in the Republic of Macedonia and that brought about change in the senior personnel in the Ministry of the Interior. And I believe in follow-up to this, since we were established by the prior political government, I believe that this was why in February 2003, one of the senior officers came and told us that we will not work any longer until we are called to work again and that we will return to our previous job posts that we held previously.

utterances.speaker: MR. DOBBYN
utterances.text: Yesterday when you were talking about the work of this working group you testified that for an investigation to commence, an injured party or a relative of an injured party had to report the incident to the local police station, and I believe this is at transcript page 8879. Is that an accurate summary of what your testimony was?

utterances.speaker: IGNO STOJKOV [Resumed]
utterances.text: Well, whenever a crime is reported, that should go through the police station or the department for internal affairs of that police station, so it was not only in the work of our working group. This is the normal course that the police takes when intervening in other cases.

utterances.speaker: MR. DOBBYN
utterances.text: So is it always necessary for a complaint to be made before an investigation can be commenced?

utterances.speaker: IGNO STOJKOV [Resumed]
utterances.text: What would be another way to learn that something had happened, whether the complaint initially comes -- I'm now speaking about the basic rule. Some aggrieved party can call the police station by phone or use the police hot line, 192, that is operating in the Republic of Macedonia and can report any case. After the case is reported, the duty officer, the duty police officer, takes the data from the complainant and enters them in the daily log-book. And after that, those police officers or inspectors who go to an on-site inspection make an Official Note that they have gone and investigated the claims.

utterances.speaker: MR. DOBBYN
utterances.text: Thank you for that but perhaps let me be a bit more specific and let me ask you: What if there's a situation where there's a crime which is notorious, which is known throughout the area or the country, which features in the media but where victims are too scared to come forward? Are you saying that in that situation the crime would not be investigated?

utterances.speaker: IGNO STOJKOV [Resumed]
utterances.text: I think that if there had been such event in my country, in the Republic of Macedonia, certainly a way would have been found to investigate the case, to arrive at the basic data, what had happened and what needs to be undertaken. However, I don't think anything of the sort had happened thus far without it being detected, without the perpetrators being identified and without the case being clarified.

utterances.speaker: MR. DOBBYN
utterances.text: I would just like to clarify the last part of your answer. Are you saying that you are not aware of any situations where investigations did take place based on media reports or general information that something had happened?

utterances.speaker: IGNO STOJKOV [Resumed]
utterances.text: This is exactly what I said. If something like that had happened, if public had learned about it, then certainly some measures had been taken to solve the case and to identify the perpetrators.

utterances.speaker: MR. DOBBYN
utterances.text: Thank you. And to move on, I'd just like to ask you: What sort of involvement, if any, did Minister Boskoski have in the working group?

utterances.speaker: IGNO STOJKOV [Resumed]
utterances.text: Mr. Boskoski, in addition to being the person signed -- who has signed by decision appointing me as member of that working group, I had no other contacts with him. My contacts in my capacity of member of that working group went either through the coordinator, Apostol Stojanovski, through the director, Goran Mitevski, and in some meetings there was also the then state secretary, Mr. Spasen Sofeski. So I never had any contacts with Mr. Boskoski, when he was a minister, during that period, before or afterwards.

utterances.speaker: MR. DOBBYN
utterances.text: You did testify yesterday that you were told the working group had Minister Boskoski's full support. And this is at transcript page 8888. What did you take that to mean?

utterances.speaker: IGNO STOJKOV [Resumed]
utterances.text: When I attended brief meetings at Mr. Mitevski, the director's office, when we reported on the progress made and tasks completed, he told us that our then minister, Mr. Ljube Boskoski, shows a great interest in the work of the group, and that we will be provided with any assistance from other bodies as well as technical assistance, which would mean vehicles, equipment, anything that we would need. I stated this yesterday.

utterances.speaker: MR. DOBBYN
utterances.text: And do you know if he, in any way, directed or influenced which cases the working group would investigate?

utterances.speaker: IGNO STOJKOV [Resumed]
utterances.text: As I told you, you can see from the decision I was the lowest ranking among my colleagues in that working group. The other colleagues had higher ranks. That means that my communication went through my coordinator or through the director, when he called me. So I am unable to know whether the then minister, Mr. Ljube Boskoski, specifically gave any orders to process some cases or not. It did not reach me. I had my superior officers and I took my orders from them.

utterances.speaker: MR. DOBBYN
utterances.text: Well, did you have any indication or any knowledge of whether he was kept informed of the progress of the working group's various investigations?

utterances.speaker: IGNO STOJKOV [Resumed]
utterances.text: Well, certainly the director, Mr. Mitevski, the then director, he certainly informed the minister because he was the one in contact with him. I'm telling you that following the line, the hierarchy that we have in the Ministry of the Interior, I could not have had without being invited by the minister gone to a meeting or a briefing with him. He was certainly informed by -- of the work of the working group but how and by whom, I don't know.

utterances.speaker: MR. DOBBYN
utterances.text: Well, can you tell me who the director, Mr. Mitevski -- actually, let me just take a step back. Am I correct in understanding that Mr. Mitevski was the person who oversaw or who was in charge of the working group?

utterances.speaker: IGNO STOJKOV [Resumed]
utterances.text: My direct superior was the coordinator, our coordinator, Apostol Stojanovski. On several occasions, Mr. Mitevski invited me alone or accompanied by Mr. Apostol Stojanovski, when he was specifically interested to learn what was the progress he asked us to report, what was completed, what was not completed, and what is yet to be taken, if this is what you wanted me to tell you.

utterances.speaker: MR. DOBBYN
utterances.text: What was the formal position of Apostol Stojanovski?

utterances.speaker: IGNO STOJKOV [Resumed]
utterances.text: Mr. Apostol Stojanovski was the chief inspector in the homicide department with the Ministry of the Interior and he was appointed member. I saw him in the working group.

utterances.speaker: MR. DOBBYN
utterances.text: And who did Mr. Stojanovski report to?

utterances.speaker: IGNO STOJKOV [Resumed]
utterances.text: Well, Mr. Stojanovski, on the basis of his job position, was the -- accountable to his superior officer, while as a member of the working group he certainly submitted the reports to his superior, or, on several occasions, because I went with him to the then under-secretary of the Ministry of Interior. That office was held by Spasen Sofeski and before him by Zivko Petrovski, but I'm not certain about this.

utterances.speaker: MR. DOBBYN
utterances.text: When you say Mr. Stojanovski was accountable to his superior officer, who was his superior officer, is this Spasen Sofeski or is it someone else that you're referring to?

utterances.speaker: IGNO STOJKOV [Resumed]
utterances.text: Mr. Apostol Stojanovski based on his job post belonged to the homicide department of the Ministry of the Interior so he certainly had his superior officer. The then head of the homicide department. I don't know who was the holder of that office at that time because I had no contact with them. But as a member of the working group, I know that he contacts with the then under-secretary, and the then director Goran Mitevski. And I know that very frequently some of the materials were taken and handed over to Mrs. Katica Jovanovska. And who was his direct superior, I don't know. I know that he was the coordinator for us, the other members of the group.

utterances.speaker: MR. DOBBYN
utterances.text: Let me ask you: Do you know who Spasen Sofeski took his orders from?

utterances.speaker: IGNO STOJKOV [Resumed]
utterances.text: Well, based on the hierarchy, the then under-secretary belonged or had as his superior officer, the director. So certainly it was Goran Mitevski.

utterances.speaker: MR. DOBBYN
utterances.text: Thank you. I'd like to move on to the next topic from there. Perhaps if you could turn to tab 4 in your binder. And do you see some photographs in front of you?

utterances.speaker: IGNO STOJKOV [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. DOBBYN
utterances.text: And if you look at the first one, which -- this is it 65 ter 1133 and the first photograph has the ERN N005-8223. And can you see, Mr. Stojkov, that this photograph shows a collection of files or boxes of files, and there are what appear to be three tan boxes stacked on top of each other. There is one blue or grey box and there are also some red binders or files stacked on top of each other. Do you recognise these at all?

utterances.speaker: IGNO STOJKOV [Resumed]
utterances.text: Well, these three boxes that you described and red folders in the background I am able to recognise. With regards to the grey box, I don't recognise that.

utterances.speaker: MR. DOBBYN
utterances.text: And what do you recognise the tan or brown boxes and the red folders as?

utterances.speaker: IGNO STOJKOV [Resumed]
utterances.text: These are part of the binders, just a few of them. There were more. They -- that is my handwriting on them. I recognise my own handwriting.

utterances.speaker: MR. DOBBYN
utterances.text: And these are the binders from where?

utterances.speaker: IGNO STOJKOV [Resumed]
utterances.text: There are binders where we placed the documents from the working groups, part of the documents. There were several binders. This is just a part of them. As far as I can see, that is my handwriting and in it it is stated "Tetovo region," as far as I can see. Kidnapped, missing persons - that is my handwriting.

utterances.speaker: MR. DOBBYN
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MR. DOBBYN
utterances.text: I would seek to tender this photograph at this time.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE PARKER
utterances.text: It will be received.

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: As Exhibit P562, Your Honours.

utterances.speaker: MR. DOBBYN
utterances.text: And can we move to the next photograph in this array, which is ERN N005-8224. And if we could just zoom in on the label.

utterances.speaker: MR. DOBBYN
utterances.text: And, Mr. Stojkov, does this label read: Evidence material from military crimes in the territory of the Republic of Macedonia?

utterances.speaker: IGNO STOJKOV [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, that is correct.

utterances.speaker: MR. DOBBYN
utterances.text: So would you agree that it appears that this box also holds files from the working group that you were part of?

utterances.speaker: IGNO STOJKOV [Resumed]
utterances.text: I can't say what is inside the box because I can't see that. But based on the heading here, I suppose that there are evidence materials on war crimes inside.
